Hey all, I wanted to point folks towards a branch which has computational cryptography proofs in a way that I think is consistent with the rigor we have in CSLib. I use Oracle TMs and I unify those with the rest of CSLib's TMs. Further, I designed a ppt tactic which allows us to prove that a reduction runs in probabilistic polynomial time without really writing much of a proof, it basically just runs through a bunch of PPT closure rules in a clever way.

On the branch, I prove quite substantial things: one way permutations imply the existence of pseudorandom generators, and one way functions imply the existence of pseudorandom generators. This branch is _way_ ahead of where CSLib is today, but I wanted to stake out this path for our cryptography such that if we start to make more progress on that, we can do it in the way that is consistent with the literature.

Here is the branch: https://github.com/SamuelSchlesinger/cslib/tree/crypto/Cslib/Crypto

There is a README there which should be quite helpful in understanding how it all fits together.
To be clear, you still write your programs in a nice free monad which is basically a probabilistic programming language. You just also discharge Oracle TM proofs about efficiency of the reductions.

I think you might know about VCVio already, but this is exactly what they do. CC : @Quang Dao

They already upstreamed free monads with PFunctors for this purpose.

Yes, much of the ideas overlap, I have contributed to VCVio. My impression is that my work is filling in the gap for the computational side, where things are very incomplete in VCVio. My impression is that it is quite possible to synthesize my PPT approach with many of the proofs and definitions in VCVio.
Looks like @Devon Tuma is thinking about similar things recently: https://github.com/Verified-zkEVM/VCVio/blob/main/docs/design/computational-complexity-spike.md
The PolyFun side has a more up to date roadmap that I think is even closer to what you are thinking I think: https://github.com/Verified-zkEVM/PolyFun/issues/279
My goal has been to get the FreeM complexity reduced to the complexity of pure Lean functions, so that work on TMs or whatever else cslib decides to support can plug in naturally
Thanks for pointing to that.
I really hope we can do crypto theory work inside of CSLib as well at some point given that aspects of crypto theory interplay with complexity theory in important ways.
Most of my current work is on integration with Std.WP but I plan to focus on this after

Sam Schlesinger said:

I really hope we can do crypto theory work inside of CSLib as well at some point given that aspects of crypto theory interplay with complexity theory in important ways.

My thought would be that both PolyFun and VCVio can trickle upstream over time, much of the general theory does belong here. Ideally the slow upstreaming trickle both improves quality of canonicalized CSlib definitions and lets people downstream move and expirement faster on things, sort of acting as a stable bridge for people

much of the general theory does belong here

Can you explain your thought process behind that?
On my end, I would like to transition us to a world where the general theory lives in CSLib and applications and "leaf proofs" live outside.
I have a few PRs open to upstreaming things. I just don't think there is maintainer bandwidth to try and upstream at the rate we get new PRs
This is more a medium term thought as the theory moves upstream, writing e.g. ArkLib proofs directly from cslib theory just still needs a lot of upstreaming is all

As it happens, I also used FreeM for TMs a while ago. I think they work best with my state monad based interpreter: put the Config and visited cell set as the state type. Interpret moves in this state. That way, a FreeM program cannot cheat at all
Ok, I will try to make progress on those PRs Devon.

I think the PPT tactic is compatible with my plan of going forward with the upper bounds proofs for TMs (both for time and space) and it would be great to generalize the tactic to other classes of functions and operations they are closed under. I will try to take a closer look at the oracle part next week.
I think actually https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/Mathlib/Tactic/FunProp.html is the right thing to use, I've been ripping it out and replacing it with that.
It runs incredibly fast I have been extremely pleased.

So yes, we should generally try to use the various types of automation and generalize it as needed. We might need to focus on specific reduction classes, but I bet we could factor it in a nice way where we reduce repeated work.

Yeah, don't take the specific way I'm doing the Oracle as gospel, feel free to propose a better one. I just want that for cryptographic security definitions such that I can define them with respect to several operations that do certain things to a state machine, like issuing signatures or whatever it might be depending on what kind of crypto we are talking about.

The core invariant I care about is separating computational proofs to a plumbing section with heavy automation and then letting the crypto look like "regular old Lean", even though in practice you might need to constrain how you program to let the automation work appropriately.
And I think this should be true for most of complexity theory as well hopefully.

Thanks @Sam Schlesinger How does your work related to complexity in EasyCrypt? https://dl.acm.org/doi/full/10.1145/3589962

I have a small experiment along those lines in CatCrypt (not yet public).
https://github.com/spitters/CatCrypt-core/

Oh funny, I never saw that paper but in my complexitylib library I do lots of Hoare Logic sorts of things. The work is targeting the same types of assurances, indeed, proofs of security/privacy in the computational model.

Got a chance to read that paper tonight. The main difference is that we model the theory as it is in the literature, based on Turing machines with machine witnesses for PPT, we don't abstract out the underlying model. We'll also use circuits for non-uniform adversaries where applicable.
The goal I want to meet is to actually implement the underlying cryptography theory relatively faithfully.
In terms of the proof ergonomics, we can support their model via a DSL.
